title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamicsfor Efficient Image Generation

paper.title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy
for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token
computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key
challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and
which should be preserved for subsequent computation.
Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures.
However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence.
In this work, we propose D ynamics- a ware T oken Me rging (DaTMe) ,
a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the
underlying diffusion dynamics.
Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information.
To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics-aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised
estimate.
The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details.
Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both
temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates.
Experiments on PixArt- α \alpha and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 34 , 29 ] have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality image [ 30 , 8 , 4 ] and video synthesis [ 20 , 17 , 31 ] , owing to their strong fidelity and scalability. However, their iterative denoising process incurs substantial computational cost, as a large number of tokens are repeatedly processed at every inference step [ 43 ] . To address this, token merging [ 2 ] has emerged as an effective training-free acceleration strategy that groups similar tokens, merges them into representative tokens, and uses the merged representations in subsequent layers [ 43 , 2 , 46 , 24 , 9 ] . For example, early token merging methods such as ToMeSD [ 2 ] first construct local merge candidate groups in a content-agnostic manner, and then form merge pairs simply based on feature similarity within each group. Consequently, content-relevant tokens can be selected as merge sources, causing local details to be absorbed and leading to visual distortion [ 43 ] . This raises a central challenge: which tokens should be absorbed through merging , and which must be retained as anchors for subsequent computation. Prior work [ 43 ] leverages classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 12 ] as a token importance signal, identifying tokens strongly steered by the text condition through the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional noise predictions as anchors to be retained. However, as shown in Fig. 1 (a), CFG-based merging tends to underprotect non-prompt regions of the image, losing fine details and structural coherence. We attribute this to CFG’s prompt-centric bias: by focusing exclusively on text-conditioned influence, CFG overlooks two key aspects of how diffusion models generate images. First, CFG fails to capture time-varying token importance . Diffusion generation follows a coarse-to-fine progression [ 10 , 13 ] , where tokens undergoing large inter-step changes represent regions in which the model is actively injecting details [ 3 ] . In this context, prematurely merging such still-evolving tokens directly attenuates their ongoing refinement by averaging their features with neighboring tokens. Crucially, the spatial distribution of these actively evolving tokens is time-varying: while it remains concentrated on foreground objects in early steps, it progressively expands toward broader spatial regions, including non-prompt areas, at later timesteps (Fig. 1 (b)). High-ranked tokens in CFG importance signal, however, remain anchored to foreground objects throughout the entire timestep, confining its search for important tokens only to prompt-aligned regions. As a result, CFG fails to identify the very tokens that should be protected: actively evolving tokens outside the foreground are prematurely merged into nearby or similar tokens, suppressing their distinct updates. Figure 1: (a) Comparison under different compression ratios. CFG-based merging [ 43 ] often overlooks background details and structures, whereas our method better preserves background integrity. (b) Spatial distribution of top-ranked tokens over denoising timesteps. CFG-based importance remains concentrated on the foreground object with limited temporal variation. In contrast, our score-based signals (Score Slope and Tweedie Diff) progressively shift from object regions to fine-grained spatial details, better matching the pseudo-GT pattern. Here, pseudo-GT is defined as the difference between the final denoised latent and the Tweedie estimate at each timestep. (c) Non-prompt region blind spot. Low-ranked tokens under the CFG-based signal consistently overlap with structurally salient regions in text-irrelevant areas (red). Second, CFG is insensitive to prompt-independent structural importance . To produce natural and coherent images, diffusion models actively generate scene elements that are not directly mentioned in the prompt such as background objects and supporting structures [ 34 , 29 ] . Although these prompt-independent structures contribute little to text guidance, they carry essential structural information such as boundaries between homogeneous regions, edges of background objects, and fine textures that anchor visual coherence. However, because CFG only measures text-conditioned discrepancy, structural boundaries in such non-prompt regions tend to receive low scores across all timesteps (Fig. 1 (c)), making them vulnerable to merging into neighboring homogeneous areas. Taken together, these observations indicate that token importance should not be defined solely by text relevance, but by diffusion dynamics: how unresolved a token remains and how much structural information it carries at the current denoising step [ 48 ] . To faithfully capture diffusion dynamics, we define two complementary signals that quantify the spatiotemporal dynamics of each token during denoising. For temporal dynamics, we start from the score function [ 41 ] , which quantifies how each token is updated at the current denoising step. In particular, we project this score into clean-image space via the Tweedie denoised estimate [ 33 , 7 ] , and use its inter-step difference as the temporal signal , assigning high values to tokens that are unresolved. Unlike CFG, this score-derived signal reflects the actual update applied to every token, regardless of prompt relevance, providing an image-wide view of generative activity (Fig. 1 (b)). For the structural signal , we measure the residual between the Tweedie estimate and its coarse-scale smoothed version, which acts as a high-pass filter highlighting structural components throughout the image. This captures prompt-independent structural boundaries, including weakly conditioned structures that CFG often underestimates. By jointly modeling temporal evolution and structural saliency, we obtain a dynamics-aware token importance signal that guides merging decisions. Building on this dynamics-aware importance, we propose D ynamics- a ware T oken Me rging (DaTMe) , a training-free token merging framework for diffusion transformers [ 29 , 4 , 19 ] . At each denoising step, DaTMe assigns token roles at the intersection of the temporal and structural signals. High-scoring tokens are assigned as constraint tokens and excluded from merging as dynamically or structurally important regions, while low-scoring tokens are assigned as source tokens from relatively stable and homogeneous regions that can be safely merged. To meet the target compression budget, DaTMe supplements the source set with grid-based spatial sampling, preventing local collapse. The resulting source tokens are then merged only within nearby regions via locality-constrained matching, built upon [ 43 ] . We primarily evaluate DaTMe on PixArt- α \alpha and FLUX, where it outperforms prior methods while maintaining visual fidelity across the entire image. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce a dynamics-aware importance map derived from the Tweedie estimate, jointly capturing the temporal evolution and structural saliency of each token. • We propose DaTMe , a training-free token merging framework that leverages the proposed temporal and spatial importance signals to identify safely mergeable tokens while preserving structurally critical regions. • We validate DaTMe on DiT (PixArt- α \alpha ) and MM-DiT (FLUX), showing strong preservation of image-wide details and state-of-the-art performance across most metrics.

sections.heading: 2 Related Works
sections.text: Token Reduction in Large Models. Token reduction is a widely used strategy for improving Transformer efficiency, mainly through token pruning or token merging [ 2 , 32 , 5 , 45 , 47 ] . Representative methods such as ToMe [ 1 ] use training-free bipartite matching, while later approaches refine token selection using attention or frequency-domain cues [ 45 , 47 ] . However, most of these methods target single-forward-pass architectures with relatively static token importance. Diffusion models, by contrast, update token representations over many steps, motivating diffusion-specific approaches such as ToMeSD [ 2 ] . Token Merging in Diffusion Models. A wide range of methods have been proposed to accelerate diffusion models, including improved samplers [ 26 , 37 , 28 , 39 , 40 ] and weight quantization [ 21 , 38 ] . However, such approaches often require additional training or optimization, introducing non-trivial overhead. Training-free methods instead reduce the number of tokens processed during inference through pruning [ 48 , 15 ] , caching [ 27 , 42 , 23 ] , or merging [ 43 , 2 , 46 , 24 , 9 ] . Among them, ToMeSD [ 2 ] extends token merging in ViTs [ 1 ] to diffusion models by grouping tokens based on feature similarity. Several subsequent methods [ 24 , 9 ] leverage cross-attention maps to identify important tokens from semantically or structurally salient regions, aiming not merely to reduce computation but also to preserve informative representations during token reduction [ 18 ] . More recently, [ 43 ] uses classifier-free guidance (CFG) as a saliency signal without additional attention computation, but because CFG primarily reflects alignment with the conditioning signal, it fails to capture the spatially heterogeneous and temporally evolving dynamics of the full image. In contrast, our method leverages the Tweedie denoised estimate to construct a dynamics-aware importance map that captures both temporal evolution and spatial structure across the image.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Our goal is to design a token merging strategy for efficient image generation by accounting for diffusion dynamics. To this end, we first define a dynamics-aware importance signal that characterizes token importance from two complementary perspectives: temporal dynamics and structural saliency . Based on this importance map, we assign tokens into functional roles for merging, distinguishing safe merge sources and structurally important constraint tokens. We then perform locality-constrained token merging, together with grid-based source completion to satisfy the target compression ratio. In the following, we first motivate our Tweedie-based spatiotemporal importance signals (Sec. 3.2 ), and then describe how they are used in our proposed DaTMe framework (Sec. 3.3 ).

We validate the theoretical analysis above through two empirical tests: temporal autocorrelation and correlation with a pseudo-GT change measure. We first examine temporal autocorrelation to assess whether each signal remains responsive to token-wise refinement over denoising steps (Fig. 2 (b)). The CFG-based importance [ 43 ] exhibits consistently high autocorrelation across all timesteps, confirming its static nature and its bias toward fixed, prompt-aligned foreground regions, as previously observed in Fig. 1 (b). In contrast, both score-based signals, namely the raw score slope and the Tweedie difference, initially show noticeably lower autocorrelation, indicating greater sensitivity to image-wide refinement than CFG. However, temporal autocorrelation alone does not naturally imply that a signal reflects token-level convergence. To evaluate whether a signal faithfully reflects token-level convergence, we measure its correlation with a reference signal constructed from the per-timestep Tweedie estimate x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) \hat{x}_{0}(t) , which we treat as a proxy for the clean image following [ 36 ] . We then define the deviation between the final clean latent x 0 x_{0} and x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) \hat{x}_{0}(t) , denoted as | x 0 − x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) | |x_{0}-\hat{x}_{0}(t)| , as a pseudo-GT measure of how much each token is still expected to change. As shown in Fig. 2 (a), the cosine similarity between x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) \hat{x}_{0}(t) and the final denoised latent steadily approaches 1.0 1.0 over time, indicating that x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) \hat{x}_{0}(t) progressively approximates the final generation state. Moreover, when tokens are partitioned by their pseudo-GT magnitude, high-ranked tokens consistently exhibit larger changes across denoising steps than low-ranked ones, suggesting that this pseudo-GT provides a meaningful per-token reference for remaining change. Using this pseudo-GT, a clear difference between the two score-based signals emerges (Fig. 2 (c)). While both signals show high correlation with the pseudo-GT in the early stages, the correlation of the raw score slope drops sharply around normalized timestep 0.4 0.4 – 0.6 0.6 . Consistent with our theoretical decomposition, this degradation closely matches the range where the scale term empirically overtakes the difference term (Fig. 3 ). At the same time, the autocorrelation of the score slope rises (Fig. 2 (b)), indicating increasingly static behavior and reduced sensitivity to token-wise refinement. In contrast, by removing scale term interference, the Tweedie difference maintains both a higher correlation with the pseudo-GT and a consistently lower temporal autocorrelation throughout denoising. Taken together, these results suggest that the Tweedie difference provides a more reliable temporal signal for tracking token evolution than either the raw score slope or CFG. Tweedie Importance Map. Building on this analysis, we define the temporal importance map as the inter-step residual in predicted clean-image space: ℳ t ​ e ​ m ​ p ( t ) = | x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) − x ^ 0 ​ ( t − 1 ) | , \mathcal{M}_{temp}^{(t)}=\left|\hat{x}_{0}(t)-\hat{x}_{0}(t-1)\right|, (7) which quantifies how much the predicted clean structure is still evolving at each spatial location. This temporal map captures when each token is actively changing during denoising. However, as previously observed in Fig. 1 (c), CFG also fails to protect structurally salient tokens in non-prompt regions—those carrying essential boundary and texture information. Under CFG-based importance, such tokens consistently receive low scores throughout denoising, leading them to be mistakenly treated as safe merge candidates and causing object boundaries to be diluted (Fig. 8 ). To capture this structural property, we introduce a spatial axis derived from the same Tweedie estimate. Specifically, we use the spatial axis to distinguish structurally salient but temporally stable tokens from genuinely mergeable homogeneous regions. To this end, we define the spatial axis as the residual between x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) \hat{x}_{0}(t) and its coarse-scale approximation obtained via interpolation-based transformation [ 16 ] : ℳ s ​ p ​ a ​ t ( t ) = | x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) − UpSample × s ​ ( DownSample × s ​ ( x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) ) ) | , \mathcal{M}_{spat}^{(t)}=\left|\hat{x}_{0}(t)-\mathrm{UpSample}_{\times s}\!\Big(\mathrm{DownSample}_{\times s}\!\big(\hat{x}_{0}(t)\big)\Big)\right|, (8) where s s denotes the spatial scale used to construct the coarse approximation. This spatial map assigns high responses to contours, boundaries, and fine textures, while giving low responses to locally homogeneous regions. By combining the temporal and spatial axes, we obtain an importance signal that reflects both how tokens evolve over time and how much structural information they carry at each denoising step.

sections.heading: 3.3 Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe)
sections.text: At each timestep t t , given a target compression ratio r r , we denote the full token set as 𝒮 t ​ o ​ t \mathcal{S}_{tot} with N = | 𝒮 t ​ o ​ t | N=|\mathcal{S}_{tot}| , and aim to merge n t ​ g ​ t = ⌊ r ​ N ⌋ n_{tgt}=\lfloor rN\rfloor tokens. While feature-similarity-based merging strategies work well in U-Net-based architectures [ 34 , 30 ] , directly applying them to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) [ 29 , 8 ] often causes severe structural distortion [ 43 , 24 ] . To prevent such distortion, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), which performs three steps: (1) assigning token roles based on the proposed Figure 4: Proposed DaTMe pipeline. Using the spatiotemporal axes, DaTMe assigns token roles and performs merging within diffusion layers. spatiotemporal importance maps, (2) completing the source budget in a spatially distributed manner, and (3) performing locality-constrained spatial matching. A detailed step-by-step algorithm of DaTMe is provided in the Appendix B . Dynamics-Aware Role Assignment. Rather than imposing a hand-crafted cutoff for what should be considered important, DaTMe adaptively assigns token roles at each denoising step based on their temporal and spatial responses under the given compression ratio r r . To prevent quality degradation caused by merging temporally evolving or structurally salient tokens, we first define a conservative source set 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ⊂ 𝒮 t ​ o ​ t \mathcal{S}_{src}\subset\mathcal{S}_{tot} as the intersection of the lowest- r r fractions of tokens ranked by ℳ t ​ e ​ m ​ p \mathcal{M}_{temp} and ℳ s ​ p ​ a ​ t \mathcal{M}_{spat} . Conversely, we define a constraint set, 𝒮 c ​ o ​ n ⊂ 𝒮 t ​ o ​ t \mathcal{S}_{con}\subset\mathcal{S}_{tot} , as the intersection of the top- ( 1 − r ) (1-r) fractions of tokens on both axes, preserving tokens that are both temporally unstable and structurally salient. By preserving 𝒮 c ​ o ​ n \mathcal{S}_{con} throughout merging, we use them as structural anchors that keep critical boundaries from dissolving into surrounding regions. Spatially Distributed Source Completion. Because 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c \mathcal{S}_{src} is defined by the strict intersection of two conditions, its size n s ​ r ​ c = | 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c | n_{src}=|\mathcal{S}_{src}| is typically smaller than the target budget n t ​ g ​ t n_{tgt} (i.e., n s ​ r ​ c < n t ​ g ​ t n_{src}<n_{tgt} ). We therefore select an additional set 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c a ​ d ​ d \mathcal{S}_{src}^{add} from the remaining unassigned tokens to satisfy | 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ∪ 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c a ​ d ​ d | = n t ​ g ​ t |\mathcal{S}_{src}\cup\mathcal{S}_{src}^{add}|=n_{tgt} . To avoid concentrating these additional source tokens in a specific region—which would lead to local information loss after merging—we adopt a grid-based spatial sampling strategy. Specifically, we reshape the token sequence into a spatial feature map, partition it into P P non-overlapping grid cells, and uniformly sample ( n t ​ g ​ t − n s ​ r ​ c ) / P (n_{tgt}-n_{src})/P tokens from each cell. The final source set is then given by 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ∗ = 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ∪ 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c a ​ d ​ d \mathcal{S}_{src}^{*}=\mathcal{S}_{src}\cup\mathcal{S}_{src}^{add} . Locality-Constrained Routing. The remaining tokens, those not assigned to 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ∗ \mathcal{S}_{src}^{*} or 𝒮 c ​ o ​ n \mathcal{S}_{con} , form the destination pool 𝒟 ⊂ 𝒮 t ​ o ​ t \mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{S}_{tot} , into which 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ∗ \mathcal{S}_{src}^{*} is merged via bipartite soft matching. Because DiTs process tokens as a sequence without inherent spatial inductive bias [ 6 ] , relying purely on feature similarity can collapse spatially distant tokens and distort local spatial structure. We therefore use spatial adjacency as the matching criterion [ 43 ] , pairing each source token with its spatially nearest destination and obtaining 𝒮 m ​ e ​ r ​ g ​ e ​ d = Merge ⁡ ( 𝒟 , 𝒮 s ​ r ​ c ∗ ) \mathcal{S}_{merged}=\mathrm{Merge}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{S}_{src}^{*}) . The final output token set is 𝒮 o ​ u ​ t = 𝒮 m ​ e ​ r ​ g ​ e ​ d ∪ 𝒮 c ​ o ​ n \mathcal{S}_{out}=\mathcal{S}_{merged}\cup\mathcal{S}_{con} , with | 𝒮 o ​ u ​ t | = N − n t ​ g ​ t |\mathcal{S}_{out}|=N-n_{tgt} . By excluding 𝒮 c ​ o ​ n \mathcal{S}_{con} from both pools and restricting merging to local neighborhoods, DaTMe compensates for the weak spatial inductive bias of DiTs and preserves visual fidelity throughout merging.

sections.text: Figure 5: Qualitative comparison under compression ratio 0.5 on PixArt- α \alpha . DaTMe better preserves structural details and background content. Figure 6: Qualitative comparison under compression ratio 0.5 on FLUX. DaTMe better preserves structural details with lower quality degradation. Implementation Details and Evaluation Metrics. We primarily conduct experiments on PixArt- α \alpha [ 4 ] using 10k image-prompt pairs sampled from the COCO 2014 validation set [ 22 ] . We set the interpolation scale to s = 4 s=4 , and for grid-based source completion, we use P = 4 P=4 grid cells. We evaluate three compression ratios: 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. Following [ 43 ] , we apply DaTMe to the middle-range self-attention layers of the DiT [ 29 ] backbone. To further evaluate scalability on a larger DiT model, we apply DaTMe to FLUX [ 19 ] . We use FLUX.1-dev and additionally apply DaTMe from the middle block to the final block within the joint-attention blocks using the same hyperparameters. More details are in the supplementary materials. For evaluation, we follow prior work [ 43 , 2 , 24 , 9 ] and report CLIP-T and FID. In addition, we report HPSv2 [ 44 ] , which complements CLIP-T by measuring preference-oriented prompt faithfulness and perceptual quality. We also report SSIM, PSNR, and LPIPS to measure image-level fidelity and detail preservation relative to the original output. We further report the Aesthetic score using Aesthetic Predictor V2.5, a SigLIP-based reference-free image aesthetic predictor. All experiments are conducted on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. sections.heading: 4.1 Main Experiments
sections.text: Qualitative Results. In Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 , we compare qualitative results at a compression ratio of 0.5. On PixArt- α \alpha , directly merging tokens based on feature similarity (ToMeSD) severely disrupts spatial structure, often leading to obvious structural distortion. Although the CFG-based method preserves foreground structures that are explicitly described in the prompt, it shows noticeably weaker preservation in background and other weakly conditioned regions, as highlighted by the red boxes. This qualitatively supports our analysis that CFG-based importance is strongly biased toward prompt-conditioned content and is therefore less effective at preserving the full image context. On FLUX, existing methods generally preserve the coarse prompt semantics, but still introduce noticeable deviations from the original generation. ToMeSD tends to alter the original composition, object geometry, or viewpoint, as seen in the relative arrangement of the cats, the fire hydrant structure, and the airplane viewpoint. ToMA shows similar structural drift while additionally introducing noisy visual degradation that weakens overall image quality. In contrast, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the original spatial configuration and object structure while maintaining the intended prompt semantics. These results demonstrate that DaTMe reduces both structural deviation and visual degradation across different architectures. Additional results under various compression ratios are in Appendix C . Quantitative Results. In Tab. 2 and Tab. 2 , we compare DaTMe with prior methods on PixArt- α \alpha [ 4 ] under various compression ratios. Although DaTMe is slightly slower than prior methods in terms of latency, the prior methods suffer from substantial quality degradation as the compression ratio increases, particularly in FID. In contrast, DaTMe remains much more robust under compression, consistently preserving image quality and achieving the most favorable overall quality-efficiency trade-off. Notably, DaTMe also attains substantially stronger structural preservation, which indicates that the proposed spatiotemporal importance signal effectively prevents structurally important tokens from being merged prematurely (Tab. 2 ). In the FLUX results, CFG-based token selection is not applicable because FLUX does not employ CFG, whereas DaTMe remains directly applicable despite the architectural difference. Across all compression ratios, DaTMe consistently achieves the strongest CLIP-T and HPSv2 scores while maintaining comparable inference efficiency (Tab. 4 ). Although ToMeSD preserves reasonable text–image alignment, its substantially lower SSIM and PSNR and higher LPIPS indicate larger structural deviations from the original generation. ToMA better preserves the original structure than ToMeSD, but still exhibits noticeable visual degradation, particularly in fine details and overall image quality. In contrast, DaTMe achieves the strongest overall image fidelity, consistently improving SSIM, PSNR, and aesthetic quality while maintaining strong prompt alignment (Tab. 4 ). These quantitative trends are consistent with Fig. 6 , where DaTMe more faithfully preserves the original image structure.

The CFG-based signal [ 43 ] is strongly biased toward prompt-aligned foreground regions and therefore neglects unmentioned background content. Using only the temporal signal alleviates this issue by preserving evolving background regions (yellow box), but it still misses structurally important boundaries (black regions), leading to structural distortions (red box). By jointly modeling temporal and spatial signals, our importance map preserves both evolving background content and critical object boundaries, resulting in more faithful image structure and higher overall visual quality. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented DaTMe , a diffusion-dynamics-aware token merging framework for efficient image generation. By leveraging the Tweedie denoised estimate, DaTMe defines token importance along two complementary axes—temporal evolution and structural saliency—that reflect the image generation process. This allows DaTMe to identify safely mergeable tokens while preserving structurally critical regions, achieving strong image fidelity and favorable quality-efficiency trade-offs across DiT-based diffusion models. Our work shows that grounding token merging in the underlying generation dynamics is a key step toward faithful and efficient diffusion inference.

Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation SeungJu ChaYe-Chan KimHyunGee KimSungho Koh Dong-Jin KimHanyang University, South Korea Email: {sju9020, dpcksdl78, khjiiii2002, ksh000906, djdkim}@hanyang.ac.kr $†$ Corresponding author Abstract Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose D ynamics- a ware T oken Me rging (DaTMe) , a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics-aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt- α \alpha and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe . 1 Introduction Diffusion models [ 34 , 29 ] have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality image [ 30 , 8 , 4 ] and video synthesis [ 20 , 17 , 31 ] , owing to their strong fidelity and scalability. However, their iterative denoising process incurs substantial computational cost, as a large number of tokens are repeatedly processed at every inference step [ 43 ] . To address this, token merging [ 2 ] has emerged as an effective training-free acceleration strategy that groups similar tokens, merges them into representative tokens, and uses the merged representations in subsequent layers [ 43 , 2 , 46 , 24 , 9 ] . For example, early token merging methods such as ToMeSD [ 2 ] first construct local merge candidate groups in a content-agnostic manner, and then form merge pairs simply based on feature similarity within each group. Consequently, content-relevant tokens can be selected as merge sources, causing local details to be absorbed and leading to visual distortion [ 43 ] . This raises a central challenge: which tokens should be absorbed through merging , and which must be retained as anchors for subsequent computation. Prior work [ 43 ] leverages classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 12 ] as a token importance signal, identifying tokens strongly steered by the text condition through the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional noise predictions as anchors to be retained. However, as shown in Fig. 1 (a), CFG-based merging tends to underprotect non-prompt regions of the image, losing fine details and structural coherence. We attribute this to CFG’s prompt-centric bias: by focusing exclusively on text-conditioned influence, CFG overlooks two key aspects of how diffusion models generate images. First, CFG fails to capture time-varying token importance . Diffusion generation follows a coarse-to-fine progression [ 10 , 13 ] , where tokens undergoing large inter-step changes represent regions in which the model is actively injecting details [ 3 ] . In this context, prematurely merging such still-evolving tokens directly attenuates their ongoing refinement by averaging their features with neighboring tokens. Crucially, the spatial distribution of these actively evolving tokens is time-varying: while it remains concentrated on foreground objects in early steps, it progressively expands toward broader spatial regions, including non-prompt areas, at later timesteps (Fig. 1 (b)). High-ranked tokens in CFG importance signal, however, remain anchored to foreground objects throughout the entire timestep, confining its search for important tokens only to prompt-aligned regions. As a result, CFG fails to identify the very tokens that should be protected: actively evolving tokens outside the foreground are prematurely merged into nearby or similar tokens, suppressing their distinct updates. Figure 1: (a) Comparison under different compression ratios. CFG-based merging [ 43 ] often overlooks background details and structures, whereas our method better preserves background integrity. (b) Spatial distribution of top-ranked tokens over denoising timesteps. CFG-based importance remains concentrated on the foreground object with limited temporal variation. In contrast, our score-based signals (Score Slope and Tweedie Diff) progressively shift from object regions to fine-grained spatial details, better matching the pseudo-GT pattern. Here, pseudo-GT is defined as the difference between the final denoised latent and the Tweedie estimate at each timestep. (c) Non-prompt region blind spot. Low-ranked tokens under the CFG-based signal consistently overlap with structurally salient regions in text-irrelevant areas (red). Second, CFG is insensitive to prompt-independent structural importance . To produce natural and coherent images, diffusion models actively generate scene elements that are not directly mentioned in the prompt such as background objects and supporting structures [ 34 , 29 ] . Although these prompt-independent structures contribute little to text guidance, they carry essential structural information such as boundaries between homogeneous regions, edges of background objects, and fine textures that anchor visual coherence. However, because CFG only measures text-conditioned discrepancy, structural boundaries in such non-prompt regions tend to receive low scores across all timesteps (Fig. 1 (c)), making them vulnerable to merging into neighboring homogeneous areas. Taken together, these observations indicate that token importance should not be defined solely by text relevance, but by diffusion dynamics: how unresolved a token remains and how much structural information it carries at the current denoising step [ 48 ] . To faithfully capture diffusion dynamics, we define two complementary signals that quantify the spatiotemporal dynamics of each token during denoising. For temporal dynamics, we start from the score function [ 41 ] , which quantifies how each token is updated at the current denoising step. In particular, we project this score into clean-image space via the Tweedie denoised estimate [ 33 , 7 ] , and use its inter-step difference as the temporal signal , assigning high values to tokens that are unresolved. Unlike CFG, this score-derived signal reflects the actual update applied to every token, regardless of prompt relevance, providing an image-wide view of generative activity (Fig. 1 (b)). For the structural signal , we measure the residual between the Tweedie estimate and its coarse-scale smoothed version, which acts as a high-pass filter highlighting structural components throughout the image. This captures prompt-independent structural boundaries, including weakly conditioned structures that CFG often underestimates. By jointly modeling temporal evolution and structural saliency, we obtain a dynamics-aware token importance signal that guides merging decisions. Building on this dynamics-aware importance, we propose D ynamics- a ware T oken Me rging (DaTMe) , a training-free token merging framework for diffusion transformers [ 29 , 4 , 19 ] . At each denoising step, DaTMe assigns token roles at the intersection of the temporal and structural signals. High-scoring tokens are assigned as constraint tokens and excluded from merging as dynamically or structurally important regions, while low-scoring tokens are assigned as source tokens from relatively stable and homogeneous regions that can be safely merged. To meet the target compression budget, DaTMe supplements the source set with grid-based spatial sampling, preventing local collapse. The resulting source tokens are then merged only within nearby regions via locality-constrained matching, built upon [ 43 ] . We primarily evaluate DaTMe on PixArt- α \alpha and FLUX, where it outperforms prior methods while maintaining visual fidelity across the entire image. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce a dynamics-aware importance map derived from the Tweedie estimate, jointly capturing the temporal evolution and structural saliency of each token. • We propose DaTMe , a training-free token merging framework that leverages the proposed temporal and spatial importance signals to identify safely mergeable tokens while preserving structurally critical regions. • We validate DaTMe on DiT (PixArt- α \alpha ) and MM-DiT (FLUX), showing strong preservation of image-wide details and state-of-the-art performance across most metrics. 2 Related Works Token Reduction in Large Models. Token reduction is a widely used strategy for improving Transformer efficiency, mainly through token pruning or token merging [ 2 , 32 , 5 , 45 , 47 ] . Representative methods such as ToMe [ 1 ] use training-free bipartite matching, while later approaches refine token selection using attention or frequency-domain cues [ 45 , 47 ] . However, most of these methods target single-forward-pass architectures with relatively static token importance. Diffusion models, by contrast, update token representations over many steps, motivating diffusion-specific approaches such as ToMeSD [ 2 ] . Token Merging in Diffusion Models. A wide range of methods have been proposed to accelerate diffusion models, including improved samplers [ 26 , 37 , 28 , 39 , 40 ] and weight quantization [ 21 , 38 ] . However, such approaches often require additional training or optimization, introducing non-trivial overhead. Training-free methods instead reduce the number of tokens processed during inference through pruning [ 48 , 15 ] , caching [ 27 , 42 , 23 ] , or merging [ 43 , 2 , 46 , 24 , 9 ] . Among them, ToMeSD [ 2 ] extends token merging in ViTs [ 1 ] to diffusion models by grouping tokens based on feature similarity. Several subsequent methods [ 24 , 9 ] leverage cross-attention maps to identify important tokens from semantically or structurally salient regions, aiming not merely to reduce computation but also to preserve informative representations during token reduction [ 18 ] . More recently, [ 43 ] uses classifier-free guidance (CFG) as a saliency signal without additional attention computation, but because CFG primarily reflects alignment with the conditioning signal, it fails to capture the spatially heterogeneous and temporally evolving dynamics of the full image. In contrast, our method leverages the Tweedie denoised estimate to construct a dynamics-aware importance map that captures both temporal evolution and spatial structure across the image. 3 Method Our goal is to design a token merging strategy for efficient image generation by accounting for diffusion dynamics. To this end, we first define a dynamics-aware importance signal that characterizes token importance from two complementary perspectives: temporal dynamics and structural saliency . Based on this importance map, we assign tokens into functional roles for merging, distinguishing safe merge sources and structurally important constraint tokens. We then perform locality-constrained token merging, together with grid-based source completion to satisfy the target compression ratio. In Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 , we compare qualitative results at a compression ratio of 0.5. On PixArt- α \alpha , directly merging tokens based on feature similarity (ToMeSD) severely disrupts spatial structure, often leading to obvious structural distortion. Although the CFG-based method preserves foreground structures that are explicitly described in the prompt, it shows noticeably weaker preservation in background and other weakly conditioned regions, as highlighted by the red boxes. This qualitatively supports our analysis that CFG-based importance is strongly biased toward prompt-conditioned content and is therefore less effective at preserving the full image context. On FLUX, existing methods generally preserve the coarse prompt semantics, but still introduce noticeable deviations from the original generation. ToMeSD tends to alter the original composition, object geometry, or viewpoint, as seen in the relative arrangement of the cats, the fire hydrant structure, and the airplane viewpoint. ToMA shows similar structural drift while additionally introducing noisy visual degradation that weakens overall image quality. In contrast, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the original spatial configuration and object structure while maintaining the intended prompt semantics. These results demonstrate that DaTMe reduces both structural deviation and visual degradation across different architectures. Additional results under various compression ratios are in Appendix C . In Tab. 5 , we ablate the two components of our importance map by using only the temporal axis, only the spatial axis, or both. As shown in Tab. 5 , this substitution consistently degrades all evaluation metrics, and Fig. 7 shows that it also introduces noticeable visual artifacts. This is consistent with our earlier analysis that the score slope becomes increasingly contaminated by schedule-driven effects in later denoising steps, making it less reliable for token merging. Fig. 8 further illustrates how different importance signals affect region preservation. The CFG-based signal [ 43 ] is strongly biased toward prompt-aligned foreground regions and therefore neglects unmentioned background content. Using only the temporal signal alleviates this issue by preserving evolving background regions (yellow box), but it still misses structurally important boundaries (black regions), leading to structural distortions (red box). By jointly modeling temporal and spatial signals, our importance map preserves both evolving background content and critical object boundaries, resulting in more faithful image structure and higher overall visual quality.
